Three climb angle layers reflect differences in climb capability among aircraft. Four weighting scenarios between obstacles and wind reveal how operational priority affects the preferred departure direction. In an application to Suseo station and the Jamsil heliport in Seoul, steeper climbs widened the usable azimuths from 8.9 to 34.4% and from 66.1 to 83.6%, respectively. By relaxing obstacle constraints, steeper climbs also shifted the preferred direction toward the prevailing wind at lower wind weights. These results show that vertiport departure paths should be planned as a set of candidate directions matched to the obstacles and wind of the site and the climb capability of the aircraft, rather than as a single runway style path.

title: Finite-History Outage Certification for Partially Observed Fluid Antenna Receivers
summary: Fluid antenna receivers can select a service position from partial port observations, but finite historical data leave uncertainty in the covariance used for that decision. We develop deployment-before-use reliability certification for a frozen partial-observation rule. A proper predictive density defines a history-based parameter region. Gaussian covariance envelopes, shared conditional-probability bounds and selector enclosures provide simultaneous risk bounds over continuous parameters and discontinuous port decisions. Separate history-coverage and integration budgets limit erroneous positive certification to 0.05 for a single qualification procedure under the stated stationary model and numerical assumptions. Confidence-set inclusion allows a new independent history to reuse the risk computation with the rule unchanged. In a structured Gaussian example with 32 candidate positions, five noisy probes and target outage 0.001, all 282 risk groups are qualified; the largest upper bound is 0.000999748. A separate coupled comparison gives a current-rule outage interval of $[7.6820,9.1266]\times10^{-4}$ and resolves lower outage than two observed-port controls using the same historical fit. One independently recalibrated history reuses the certificate without additional risk sampling. Unresolved and adverse-member controls delimit this reuse.

title: It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity and Limits of Continuous Encoders for Over-the-Air Computation
summary: We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.

title: Causal Syntax Circuits in CodeLMs: Budget and Probe Decide What Looks Localised
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Linguistic Principles for Foundation Models (LP4FM). All four authors contributed equally
summary: Code models write Python when the prompt does not say which language to use. We ask a mechanistic question about that habit: is it produced by a small, findable group of components inside the model? We run one pipeline---mean ablation, activation patching, greedy circuit extraction, a random-control significance test, and activation steering---over 55 model-language settings spanning ten open code models (five base and five instruction-tuned), three target languages (Rust, C#, PHP), two prompt suites, and two component budgets. We report five findings. First, the preference is large, grows with model size, and survives instruction tuning: it is larger on every instruction-tuned checkpoint than on its base version, by 12% on average. Second, its measured size is mostly a property of the probe; replacing our aligned prompts with XLCoST parallel functions takes the same measurement on the same models from about 1.6 to about 0.01. Third, whether the preference looks localised depends on how many components the search may keep: with a budget of 12, 1 of 15 settings yields a circuit that beats size-matched random controls after multiple-comparison correction, and with a budget of 40, 6 of 15 do. Fourth, interventions that a smaller-budget study reports as uniformly failing do sometimes succeed: patching makes a Python prompt prefer target syntax in 2 of 45 settings, and steering changes the most likely next token in 9 of 45. Fifth, every circuit whose effect is significant but points away from the target language comes from a setting where circuit extraction failed, which makes such results a diagnostic rather than a phenomenon. The practical lesson is that a claim about whether a behaviour is localised can turn on analysis choices that papers rarely report. We release the full grid so those choices can be varied.

title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
summary: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

title: Policy-Gradient Transfer under a Shared State Estimator
summary: This paper considers the problem of policy-gradient transfer from a simulator to a physical plant when both are controlled through the same fixed state estimator. The plant and the simulator are partially observed nonlinear systems with additive Gaussian noise of common known covariance whose dynamics and observation models differ, and the controller is a squashed Gaussian policy with uniformly bounded latent mean and first two parameter derivatives. We derive a bound on the difference between the plant and simulator policy gradients that is linear in the noise-weighted model error and requires no estimator-accuracy guarantee, because the shared estimator is a common post-processing of the measurements and the data-processing inequality compares the trajectory laws without an estimation-error term. Based on this bound, we derive an occupancy-weighted refinement, a sufficient condition for the simulator gradient to be an ascent direction for the plant, and a bound on the expected squared plant gradient at a random iterate of a finite simulator-training run with optimization, truncation and model-error terms. Simulation results on a scalar system and a pendulum are presented to validate the theoretical results.

title: Receiver-Specific Interventional Valuation of Semantic Atoms for Budget-Constrained Multi-Agent Communication
summary: Cooperative multi-agent semantic communication requires deciding not only how a transmitter encodes its observation, but also which resulting semantic content should be delivered to each receiver under a limited link budget. We introduce an encoder-agnostic transmitter-side framework for receiver-specific valuation of independently selectable semantic units, termed semantic atoms. Each atom is assigned a signed value that quantifies whether delivering it is expected to improve or degrade the intended receiver's downstream decision. We formulate this effect through a controlled-delivery utility and identify it via prospective randomized payload delivery before the receiver acts. A shadow receiver estimates this utility using only transmitter-available information, from which receiver-specific leave-one-out (LOO) and Shapley atom values are computed. Experiments on a four-receiver intersection benchmark show 68.4% accuracy in recovering the sign of non-negligible LOO atom effects and a Spearman correlation of 0.302 between estimated and reference LOO values. Under limited budgets, we show that receiver-specific selection consistently outperforms shared and random alternatives, demonstrating the benefit of adapting semantic ranking to the intended receiver. At full affordability, exhaustive subset selection also outperforms full-payload transmission, showing that transmitting all available content need not maximize receiver utility. Overall, our results show that receiver-specific semantic valuation can support effective budget-constrained communication despite imperfect atom-value estimation.

title: How Does Probabilistic Constellation Shaping Control Ranging Sidelobe Levels in ISAC?
summary: Probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS), originally designed to fill the gap between finite uniform constellations and continuous capacity-achieving input distributions, has recently emerged as a central tool in adjusting the expected integrated sidelobe level (EISL) in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). In this paper, we show that PCS goes beyond EISL: A large class of PCS methods, termed as type-based PCS, are capable of providing precise control over codeword-wise integrated sidelobe level ratio (ISLR) for systems employing orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), thus yielding a stronger sensing performance guarantee than EISL control. We further show that OFDM is almost the only unitary modulation basis whose codeword-wise ISLR can be precisely controlled by type-based PCS. Based upon the analytical results, practical type-based PCS methods compatible with the probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS) framework are conceived, which achieve higher communication rates than existing ISAC-oriented PCS methods under identical ISLR constraints.

title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
summary: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.

title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Code and aggregate data: https://github.com/bitcoindatalabs/ln-client-diversity
summary: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 84% of public nodes and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.

title: Scaling up statistical model checking of cyber-physical systems via algorithm ensemble and parallel simulations over HPC infrastructures
summary: Model-based formal verification of industry-relevant Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) is often a computationally prohibitive task. In most cases, the complexity of the models precludes any prospect of symbolic analysis, leaving numerical simulation as the only viable option. Unfortunately, exhaustive simulation of a CPS model over the entire set of plausible operational scenarios is rarely possible in practice, and alternative strategies such as Statistical Model Checking (SMC) must be used instead. In this article, we show that the number of model simulations (samples) required by SMC techniques to converge can be significantly reduced by considering multiple (an ensemble of) Adaptive Stopping Algorithms (SAs) at once, and that the simulations themselves (by far the most expensive step of the entire workload) can be efficiently sped up by exploiting massively parallel platforms. With three industry-scale CPS models, we experimentally show that the use of an ensemble of two state-of-the-art SAs (AA and EBGStop) may require dozens of millions fewer samples when compared to running a single algorithm, with reductions in sample size of up to 78%. Furthermore, we show that our implementation, by massively parallelizing system model simulations on a HPC infrastructure, yields speed-ups for the completion time of the verification tasks which are practically linear with respect to the number of computational nodes, thus achieving an efficiency of virtually 100%, even on very large platforms. This makes it possible to complete tasks of model-based SMC verification for complex CPSs in a matter of hours or days, whereas a naïve sequential execution would require from months to many years.

title: Wavefront Engineering for Physical Layer Security in Near-Field Wireless Communications
summary: With wireless transmission exposing information to potential interception by unintended receivers, physical layer security (PLS) offers a promising approach to securing wireless communications. Beamforming can mitigate this vulnerability by exploiting the spatial characteristics of wireless propagation to concentrate power toward the intended receiver while suppressing it at potential eavesdroppers. However, as wireless systems enter the radiating near field of large-aperture antenna arrays, the resulting wavefront curvature provides additional opportunities for spatial wavefront engineering to enhance PLS. In this work, we investigate the use of different beam types for PLS, including focused, curved, abruptly autofocusing, and cosine beams, generated using uniform linear and planar arrays (ULAs/UPAs). To quantify their performance, we introduce power-based metrics that characterize the power received by the legitimate user and a potential eavesdropper. For all beam types we introduce focusing along the vertical UPA direction, to independently control the phase distributions along the two UPA dimensions and enhance the power discrimination between the legitimate receiver and the eavesdropper. We also propose hollow-focused beams, in which an inactive strip is introduced in the transmitting aperture to create a protected low-power region between the transmitter and the legitimate receiver. The results demonstrate that vertical focusing dramatically enhances the PLS performance and that hollow-focused beams achieve superior PLS performance in both line-of-sight (LoS) and vicinity-of-user (VoU) scenarios.

title: Fisher Information and Support Complexity of Gaussian Mixtures
summary:
We study lower bounds on the Fisher information of Gaussian location mixtures and their applications to estimation problems. First, for a discrete mixing distribution, we derive a universal positive-semidefinite lower bound on the Fisher information matrix in terms of the Rényi entropy of order two. For a mixing distribution supported on $K$ points, this bound scales as $\log(K)/K^2$, improving by a logarithmic factor on the support-size dependence obtained from Stam's inequality. We then develop dimension-aware trace bounds using classical Sobolev inequalities. These bounds are expressed in terms of Sibson's $α$-mutual information and yield the scaling $K^{-2/n}$ in dimension $n$. A complementary bound involving the $α$-mutual information of order $1/2$ is obtained using the sharp Young convolution inequality.
  The derived inequalities are further specialized to rotationally invariant mixing distributions supported on discrete spherical shells. In this setting, an intrinsic-dimensional bound on Sibson mutual information leads to lower bounds on the Fisher information in terms of the number of occupied shells. As applications, we study least favorable priors for bounded Gaussian mean estimation. In the scalar case, we show that the least favorable prior on $[-R,R]$ has at least $Ω(R\sqrt{\log R})$ support points and that each of its probability masses is of order at most $1/R$. In the vector case, we show that the number of occupied shells grows at least linearly with $R$. Finally, Brown's identity and the I-MMSE relationship are used to translate the Fisher-information inequalities into upper bounds on the MMSE and mutual information.

title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.

title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

title: Optimal energy conversion -- A port-Hamiltonian approach
summary: This paper studies optimal energy conversion in port-Hamiltonian systems. We analyze state- and control-constrained finite-horizon optimal control problems that maximize energy conversion efficiencies. Under suitable reachability conditions, we show that the asymptotic optimal efficiencies exist and coincide with the corresponding optimal cyclic efficiencies. For a class of port-Hamiltonian systems describing coupled storage-conversion components, we further derive intrinsic limits on achievable energy conversion and establish a generalized Carnot-type efficiency bound. Our results provide an optimal-control framework connecting asymptotic optimal operation, cyclic operation, and fundamental efficiency limits for port-Hamiltonian systems.

title: From Interference to Diversity: Mode Coloring and Two-Dimensional Modal-Time Rake Combining for Multipath OAM Communications
summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) beams provide a spatial-multiplexing dimension for wireless communications, but multipath scattering broadens their mode spectrum, so that energy leaks across modes as inter-mode interference (IMI), which conventional OAM demultiplexing discards. This paper treats the leaked modal energy not as interference but as a structured, harvestable resource: it attains up to $LK$-fold asymptotic diversity under independent-branch fading and yields harvested energy under the rank-limited per-tap fading of the operating channel. Each active OAM mode is colored with a distinct time-domain orthogonal spreading code, and a two-dimensional (2D) receiver grid spanning the OAM modes and the resolvable multipath delays jointly combines the despread outputs. The design builds on the Bessel order-difference coupling law of tilted OAM beams, summarized by a Gaussian mode-diffusion model with a mode-coherence metric that quantifies the surviving orthogonality, and on an effective diversity metric that separates the combining gain available at finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) from the asymptotic diversity order. At 28~GHz, with a four-mode eight-element uniform circular array (UCA) and four resolvable multipath taps, the proposed 2D modal-time Rake lowers the bit-error rate (BER) by one to three orders of magnitude and saves roughly 10--15~dB of required SNR over mode-wise detection and mode-domain zero-forcing (ZF) and minimum mean-square error (MMSE) detection, and it also outperforms an uncolored modal-time MMSE equalizer; the advantage survives the spectral-efficiency cost of spreading as well as channel-estimation and timing imperfections.

title: Short-Boundary Signaling for Asynchronous Grant-Free Control-to-Control Communications
summary: In asynchronous grant-free access, receivers must detect variable-length transmissions and identify their start and end. Existing decoder-aided receivers use start and tail sequences which are as long as one codeword, causing substantial overhead for short commands. This paper treats the boundary (i.e., start and tail sequences) length as an independent design parameter and proposes a convolutional neural network that detects both boundaries from the received waveform and the decoder soft output. Its waveform input size decreases with the boundary length, while the decoder input keeps the codeword length, so the boundary can be shortened without altering the decoder. Analysis and simulations quantify the resulting tradeoff among payload efficiency, collision exposure, and boundary detection. The results show that the proposed receiver can exploit very short boundaries: in the considered setting, the shortest tested boundary, $L_{\mathrm{b}}=16$, yields the highest effective payload efficiency at all tested loads, whereas a correlation-based benchmark with the same sequences performs best with $L_{\mathrm{b}}=64$ at moderate and high loads.

title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.

title: Blind Watermarking of Software Repositories via Module Placement
summary: Source-code watermarking supports provenance tracking by embedding a recoverable identifier in a software artifact. Many existing approaches encode this identifier in tokens or program syntax, exposing the watermark to transformations that modify the source text. We present PlaceMark, a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within a repository. Each eligible module is identified by its filename and top-level definition names. A secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and its position in the reading order; the module's location within its candidate list determines the encoded symbol. Embedding relocates selected modules and updates their import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters, without an original copy or placement ledger. Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, while one provides no placement channel. In 216 trials of the evaluated text transformations, the payload is recovered exactly. Relocation degrades recovery gradually on Django, Airflow and Salt, while on Pylint a path-based exclusion in our implementation lets relocation change carrier membership, and we measure it for an untargeted adversary and for one that concentrates its budget on the public carrier set. Changes to filenames or definition names alter the identity input and are measured separately. Exact recovery also depends on placement feasibility. The results characterize module placement as a carrier that can complement watermarks embedded in source text.

title: Event-Triggered Data Selection for Online Frequency-Domain Identification
summary: Online identification of frequency response functions is increasingly relevant for control and monitoring of high-performance systems whose dynamics may change during operation. In modern machines, however, continuously transmitting all locally acquired measurements to a central unit for identification can impose substantial communication demands, particularly as sensing rates and the number of subsystems increase. This paper develops an event-triggered data-selection approach for remote frequency-domain identification, in which periodically acquired measurements are evaluated locally and transmitted only when relevant. The selection mechanism combines information about the current estimation uncertainty with evidence of model mismatch, reducing communication while preserving identification accuracy and responsiveness to changes in the dynamics.

title: Dual-Purpose SSB Design for Joint Time-Frequency Synchronization Using Relocated DMRS
summary: The synchronization signal block (SSB) is designed to synchronize a capable user-equipment (UE) with the base-station (BS) in recent cellular networks. However, the same SSB cannot be utilized by a narrowband, low-complexity, and low-power internet of things (IoT) device for synchronization. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a dual-purpose SSB (DP-SSB) to enable low-complexity IoT synchronization using the existing SSB, while ensuring uninterrupted conventional UE operation. Specifically, selected demodulation reference signal (DMRS) symbols are contiguously mapped to some physical resource blocks (PRBs) in the second and fourth symbols of the DP-SSB. These DMRS symbols are further optimized using a receiver-aware least square (LS) approach to impose a distinct time-domain structure at the output of the IoT front-end. At the IoT receiver, a reduced-rate observation of the DP-SSB is obtained after narrowband filtering and decimation that is exploited for energy detection and sequential time-frequency (TF) synchronization. For the UE, primary synchronization signal (PSS) and secondary synchronization signal (SSS)-based synchronization is preserved, while the effect of relocated DMRS on the channel estimation and physical broadcast channel (PBCH) reception is assessed. The performance of the proposed DP-SSB is evaluated in terms of detection probability, TF synchronization accuracy, IoT receiver computational complexity, and UE-side PBCH decoding. Simulation results validate the analytical detection characterization and demonstrate reliable low-power IoT synchronization performance compared with the benchmark synchronization schemes while maintaining conventional UE operation.

title: Model-Driven Deep Learning for Distributed Detection with Low-Bit Quantization
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted by IEEE JSAC
summary: Distributed detection plays a fundamental role in communication-efficient collaborative inference over large-scale networks, where spatially distributed nodes must cooperate using severely quantized messages due to bandwidth constraints. While low-bit quantization is essential for reducing communication overhead, it can significantly degrade detection performance, particularly when prior knowledge of observation noise is unavailable. To address this challenge, we propose a model-driven deep learning framework for distributed detection with low-bit quantization. For fixed local quantizers, we first derive the exact finite-sensor maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection error and prove that, under conditionally independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, independent local randomizations, and a common quantization-level constraint, identical quantizers preserve the supremum of the average network Chernoff information. Guided by these results, we develop a binary probabilistic quantizer with a trainable neural probability controller and design a tree-structured probabilistic quantizer for scalable multi-bit quantization. The exact finite-sensor MAP error provides the training objective for the binary quantizer, while we derive a computationally tractable Bhattacharyya surrogate objective for training the multi-bit quantizer. For both cases, we derive analytical MAP fusion rules based on the class-conditional probability mass functions (PMFs) of the quantized messages. When the observation statistics are unknown, these PMFs are estimated from held-out labeled data, yielding plug-in MAP detectors. Simulation results show that the proposed method approaches centralized-oracle performance at higher quantization resolutions and remains effective under changes in network size and test-time signal amplitude.

title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.

title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey of Thermal Side-Channel and Perception Attacks
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. These paths differ in mechanism and privilege; both exploit interfaces that AV stacks cannot disable without compromising Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF). Classical microarchitectural and cyber-physical systems (CPS) surveys address cache timing, adversarial machine learning, and camera or LiDAR spoofing; no prior survey jointly frames physical thermal IR attacks and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry as one residual-risk class. This survey systematizes thirteen representative works into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, comparing them by privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance. We distinguish attack family from adversary class and map defenses to residual risk while thermal management remains operational. A commodity proxy supports the software co-tenant branch only; physical IR evidence comes from cited literature. We identify open problems in on-target automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis, aiming to motivate co-design across sensors, operating systems, silicon, and automotive standards.

title: A Quad Beam Variable Height Antenna System for Reliable Underground Mine Tunnel Communications
summary: Mine accidents can damage the wired backbone supporting underground wireless networks, forcing rescue teams to deploy temporary mesh nodes to maintain communication with the surface. Although higher carrier frequencies can support bandwidth-intensive applications such as live video, multimode propagation within mine tunnels produces severe, spatially localized fading. Movable antennas can mitigate these fades by adjusting antenna position; however, moving all antennas on a multi-link relay node simultaneously may improve one link at the expense of another. This paper introduces QuadBeam, a compact mesh node antenna system comprising four independently positionable 2.4~GHz patch antennas mounted on the side faces of a central hub, together with a 900~MHz monopole for backup voice communication. A preliminary prototype incorporates one motor-driven patch mount and three manually adjustable mounts. Bench measurements show interelement coupling below $-46$~dB between patches on adjacent faces. Measurements at five carrier frequencies from 2.40~GHz to 2.48~GHz in the Edgar Experimental Mine reveal 19~dB to 26~dB received-power variations across transmitter and receiver separations of 8.3~m to 18.3~m. Adjusting the receiver height over approximately 20~cm yields received-power improvements of up to 22~dB. Repositioning neighboring patches and removing or reinstalling the monopole produce no noticeable change in the active link. These results demonstrate the potential of independently positioned antennas to alleviate spatial fading in underground mesh communications.

title: High-Order Sinusoidal Modeling for Precise Parameter Refinement
comment: This manuscript is currently under review for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Although the amplitude estimation of sinusoids is a linear and tractable problem when their frequencies are known, the accuracy of signal modeling is fundamentally limited by the inevitable frequency mismatches produced by existing methods. Quasi-harmonic modeling (QHM) and its extensions (aQHM and eaQHM) offer the ability to refine frequency estimates while extracting amplitudes; however, their extraction and correction capabilities remain limited. In this paper, we first revisit QHM methods from the perspective of frequency mismatches, and reveal that their performances are essentially constrained by the order of the model. Specifically, QHM methods are linear models and thus incapable of capturing higher-order frequency variations, leading to suboptimal modeling accuracy. Second, to address this limitation, we propose a higher-order modeling framework that enables more precise approximation of signal components. Eventually, we qualitatively characterize the optimization problem and employ the Levenberg--Marquardt (LM) algorithm for parameter estimation. As a result, the proposed method allows for significantly improved estimation of amplitudes, frequencies, and phases of sinusoidal components, enabling more accurate signal modeling. Experiments on both simulation study and speech signals demonstrate the superiority of the high-order model in frequency refinement and parameter extraction and its robustness under additive noise conditions.

title: Legitimate Reconstruction Advantage in Wiretapped Semantics-Aware Remote Monitoring
summary: This paper investigates joint accuracy and security in semantics-aware remote monitoring, where source updates intended for a legitimate receiver may also be intercepted by an eavesdropper. We define legitimate reconstruction advantage (LRA) as the joint event that the intended receiver correctly reconstructs the current source state using received updates while the eavesdropper reconstructs it incorrectly. Source evolution changes the relevance of received updates at the two receivers, so their marginal reconstruction accuracies do not, in general, determine the probability of this joint event. Under randomized stationary (RS) transmission and zero-order-hold reconstruction at both receivers, we derive an explicit joint stationary distribution and closed-form expressions for LRA probability and persistence for general finite-state ergodic Markov sources. For two-state and uniform-transition sources, we obtain algebraic expressions that enable low-complexity optimization of RS policies. Analytical and numerical results show that maximizing the probability of legitimate advantage need not maximize its persistence. For two-state sources, rare-transmission analysis reveals that, at a fixed sum of transition probabilities, greater transition asymmetry can increase persistence while reducing LRA probability. Moreover, optimizing marginal accuracy and security metrics can select policies that are suboptimal for LRA. Counterintuitively, more frequent transmission or improved legitimate-channel reliability can increase legitimate reconstruction accuracy while reducing LRA probability. Finally, a geofencing application translates prescribed LRA requirements into spatial constraints on eavesdropper locations.

title: Vertical Sliced Wasserstein Distances for Meta-Measures
summary: Many modern learning problems require comparing probability distributions whose individual observations are themselves probability measures, naturally giving rise to meta-measures in $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$. However, optimal transport distances on this space can be prohibitively expensive to evaluate. We introduce the vertical sliced Wasserstein ($\mathrm{VSW}$) distance, a scalable metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$. Rather than slicing along the transport geometry of $\mathcal{P}(Ω)$, $\mathrm{VSW}$ projects each inner measure using continuous test functions and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions with one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. We prove that $\mathrm{VSW}$ is a valid metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$, metrizes weak convergence, and admits dimension-independent statistical convergence guarantees. Empirically, $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides high accuracy and efficiency compared with existing distances for meta-measures. We further derive a practical particle gradient for the empirical $\mathrm{VSW}_2^2$ objective and demonstrate its use for gradient-based transport of meta-measures. $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides a simple and scalable alternative for comparing and optimizing distributions of distributions.

title: NOMAI: Scalable Federated Learning with Private Weights
summary: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.

title: A hidden Markov model for unsupervised EEG-based tracking of auditory attention to a single voice
summary:
Objective: Absolute auditory attention decoding (aAAD) aims to track how strongly a listener attends to a single speech source using electroencephalography (EEG). Unlike selective auditory attention decoding, aAAD lacks a competing speech reference, making reliable attention tracking challenging.
  Approach: We propose a fully unsupervised aAAD pipeline combining neural envelope tracking (NET) with hidden Markov model (HMM)-based temporal inference. Using EEG signals and the target speech envelope, the framework estimates a continuous attention trajectory without explicit attention-state labels. We evaluate the approach using EEG recordings from 30 adults, investigate the impact of analysis window length, and compare HMM post-processing with moving-average (MA) smoothing and alternative EEG features.
  Main results: With 1-s analysis windows, non-causal HMM post-processing improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for all 30 participants, increasing mean AUC from 0.547 for raw NET to 0.832. A 5-s window achieves the highest mean AUC of 0.858. Compared with non-causal MA smoothing, the HMM achieves higher AUC across the examined smoothing scales. Individual switch detection times are comparable, while the HMM generally achieves lower group-level detection times. NET also outperforms alpha power and spectral entropy as an observation feature in the unsupervised HMM framework.
  Significance: The proposed framework provides a label-free approach for estimating temporal fluctuations in auditory attention, demonstrating the utility of probabilistic temporal inference for continuous attention tracking in single-speaker listening scenarios.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Joint Communication and Computation in XR Systems
comment: 18 pages, 16 figures, 3 tables. This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing
summary: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.

title: Interpreting Language Model Parameters
comment: 124 pages, 47 figures. This paper was written to be read online, with interactive figures, at https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters
summary: Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover how neural networks use their parameters to implement their impressive neural algorithms. Although previous work has uncovered substantial structure in the intermediate representations that networks use, little progress has been made to understand how the parameters and nonlinearities of networks perform computations on those representations. In this work, we present a method that brings us closer to this understanding by decomposing a language model's parameters into subcomponents that each implement only a small part of the model's learned algorithm, while simultaneously requiring only a small fraction of those subcomponents to account for the network's behavior on any input. The method, adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD), optimizes for decompositions of neural network parameters into simple subcomponents that preserve the network's input-output behavior even when many subcomponents are ablated, including under ablations that are adversarially selected to destroy behavior. This encourages learning subcomponents that provide short, mechanistically faithful descriptions of the network's behavior that should aggregate appropriately into more global descriptions of the network's learned algorithm. We study how sequences of interactions between these parameter subcomponents produce the network's output on particular inputs, enabling a new kind of 'circuit' analysis. While more work remains to be done to deepen our understanding of how neural networks use their parameters to compute their behavior, our work suggests an approach to identify a small set of simple, mechanistically faithful subcomponents on which further mechanistic analysis can be based.

title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
comment: 36 pages, 13 figures, 13 tables. Code and data at https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up
summary: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

title: Stability Analysis in IBR-Dominated Grids: Model-Based and Data-Driven Methodologies
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics
summary: Stability issues in converter-dominated grids have a multifold nature, where static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena can influence each other. Capturing the interplay among these different stability aspects requires a rethinking of conventional modeling and analysis tools for power systems. As a further complication, Intellectual Property protection among manufacturers and system operators makes detailed converters and grid models unattainable. This motivates the use of data-driven approaches for stability analysis and control, nevertheless achieving an insightful representation of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena from data still leaves many open questions. This paper discusses model-based and data-driven methodologies for stability analysis of converter-dominated grids. The instability mechanisms of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena are conceptually explained, and the capability of different modeling and analysis tools to investigate them is examined. The effectiveness of data-driven methodologies to analyze instability phenomena in their multifold nature is debated, and the challenges on data completeness, model generalization under untrained conditions, physical interpretability, and uncertainty awareness are discussed.

title: Sensing-Assisted OFDM with Index Modulation: A Waveform for Optical Wireless Integrated Communication and Localisation
summary: This paper proposes sensing-assisted OFDM with index modulation (SA-OFDM-IM) for joint communication and localisation over optical wireless systems. In SA-OFDM-IM, a multilayer frequency-domain architecture partitions each layer's admissible subcarriers into disjoint communication and distributed sensing-pilot subsets, applying group-wise index modulation (IM) within the communication subset. A constrained sensing-to-communication energy allocation jointly minimises average bit-error rate (BER) and delay-based localisation root mean square error (RMSE) under a minimum power-domain margin, enabling low-complexity, ordered-energy detection of both sensing and communication subcarriers without exhaustive maximum-likelihood search. Sensing tones are aggregated across the frame to reconstruct the channel frequency response, yielding the line-of-sight (LoS) delay tap and phase-compensated LoS gain for multilateration and, via the proposed delay-aided received signal strength (RSS) refinement. Simulation results indicate that SA-OFDM-IM can achieve up to 5 dB lower SNR requirement in BER and up to three orders of magnitude lower channel-estimation error than DC-biased optical OFDM, while the RSS estimator removes the SNR-independent error floors of delay-only and hybrid-RSS benchmarks to attain sub-delay-bin range and position accuracy, remaining robust under random known and unknown receiver orientations.

title: Design of a Family of Rate-Adaptive LDPC Convolutional Codes with Short Constraint Length
summary: This paper studies the design of some high-rate, adaptive, low-density parity-check (LDPC) convolutional codes with short constraint length, based on interleaved parity-check polynomials. Starting from some known results regarding the selection of polynomials that yield codes free of short cycles in the associated Tanner graphs, we propose some new constructions based on Golomb rulers, along with relaxed variants that do not strictly satisfy the Golomb ruler condition, but retain similar structural properties. The result is a family of rate-adaptive code constructions with code rates of the form $R=(n_0-1)/n_0$. Conditions for the absence of length-4 cycles are derived, together with upper bounds on the free distance that are met in all considered examples.

title: Optimal Hydra: Model Heterogeneous Federated Learning for LLMs using Data-Informed Hydra-Nets
summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained on vast amounts of data have demonstrated impressive performance over a range of tasks, but future performance gains will require increasing amounts of data and compute. Federated Learning (FL) facilitates training on decentralized private data, but client resource limitations can make training impractical, particularly as model sizes continue to expand. These resource constraints make the assumption of a shared server-client architecture impractical. Model heterogeneous FL offers a promising alternative by adapting model size to client capabilities; however, previous work is limited to the pre-training setting, and conclusions on sub-network selection do not necessarily hold for fine-tuning. Furthermore, prior approaches create client sub-networks without considering their unique data distributions, thereby overlooking the opportunity to tailor sub-network architecture to local data. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer defined feature spaces, we propose Optimal Hydra, a transformer based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client specific attention head selection, aligned with local data distributions. Optimal Hydra makes explicit use of client data to produce client-specific sub-networks we call Hydra-nets. To our knowledge, this is the first model heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning. Experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while also reducing local resource demands.

title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
comment: Accepted to the 2027 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
summary:
We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(H)$ reaction queries, where $H$ is the entropy of the secret key.
  The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side.
  We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.

title: Sensor Diagnosis for Fuel and Emissions Monitoring in Heavy-Duty Diesel Vehicles
comment: Accepted at the Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Faulty sensor readings can distort estimates of fuel use and carbon dioxide emissions from diesel engines. We evaluate two procedures that use relationships learned from healthy measurements to diagnose faults and guide fuel correction. The diagnosis procedure tests whether replacing a suspected faulty reading with an estimated healthy value helps a model predict another sensor's recorded reading more accurately. It then predicts the fault type and decides whether to report the diagnosis. We evaluate five synthetic fault types on 217 steady-state operating points from a heavy-duty diesel engine, excluding all measurements at selected engine speeds from training. Across 31,500 fault-injected groups of 20 operating points, it issues diagnoses for 77.3% of groups, with 92.1% of diagnoses issued on these groups correct. The fuel correction procedure uses a different sensor-selection rule at individual operating points, testing how each replacement changes the largest prediction error across all six sensors. Fuel correction requires a fault alarm and engine speed and torque close to the training conditions. A fuel reading is replaced only when its replacement reduces the largest prediction error sufficiently more than replacements for the other sensors. Assuming faults in 1% of one-hour scenarios, equally likely sensors and fault types, and equal time at each measured condition, selected fuel corrections reduce mean absolute error in calculated combustion CO2 by 83.8%. On this engine map, learned relationships support complete sensor diagnoses and fuel corrections that improve emissions accounting while preserving unaffected readings.

title: Confidence-Guided Adaptive Beam Selection for Vision-Aided Beam Tracking in mmWave Systems
summary: Vision-aided beam tracking reduces mmWave beam-training overhead by predicting beam indices from camera observations. Fixed top-$K$ selection, however, assigns the same candidate beam budget to all predictions, ignoring uncertainty variations across samples and horizons. This letter proposes confidence-guided adaptive candidate selection: predictor logits are temperature-calibrated, and the smallest top-ranked beam set whose cumulative probability reaches a target threshold is retained under a maximum budget. On DeepSense~6G Scenario~8, over five random seeds and at matched overhead, the policy improves candidate set accuracy by up to 3.80 percentage points, increases normalized received power by 0.32 percentage points, and reduces outage probability by 2.06 percentage points without retraining the predictor.

title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
summary: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
summary: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation
summary: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano. Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples. Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components. We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.

title: Statistical Ambiguity-Function-Aware Joint Beamforming and Subcarrier Allocation for MIMO-OFDM ISAC under Random Symbols
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications
summary: Ambiguity function (AF) characterizes the delay--Doppler sidelobe structure that governs target resolution and masking in radar sensing. In ISAC, however, random communication symbols make the AF data-dependent, complicating its characterization and incorporation into transmit design. This raises a fundamental question: which AF characteristic can be effectively controlled through beamforming in a practical multiuser multitarget (MUMT) MIMO--OFDM system? To answer this, we statistically characterize the discrete-periodic AF (DP-AF) and derive an exact closed-form expected sidelobe level (ESL). We observe that nonzero-Doppler ESL cuts are delay-flat and the full two-dimensional integrated sidelobe level ratio (ISLR) is invariant to beamforming, whereas the zero-Doppler peak-to-sidelobe ratio (PSLR) remains controllable. We accordingly formulate an AF-aware joint beamforming and subcarrier-allocation problem with target-wise PSLR and illumination constraints. Since the direct PSLR constraint is intractable, we characterize its global optimum and prove that, for symbol kurtosis greater than one, the PSLR is maximized if and only if each target-wise directional-power profile is flat across subcarriers. We then introduce the coefficient of variation (CV) to measure deviation from this flatness and derive tight CV-dependent PSLR bounds. The lower bound yields a convex sufficient constraint for a desired PSLR, enabling an efficient reformulation. Simulations show $9.4$--$11.0$ dB worst-case PSLR gains over communication-only beamforming at the flat-spectrum point with a $2.4$--$5.9\%$ sum-rate loss. The CV-relaxed formulation achieves $99.7\%$ of the average sum-rate of the original PSLR-constrained problem, while reducing runtime by factors of $10.35$--$12.15$ under the considered scenarios.

title: The Information Bottleneck is NP-hard
summary: Given a joint distribution $P_{XY}$ on a finite alphabet, the information bottleneck method seeks a representation $T$ of $X$ that is as informative as possible about $Y$ while compressing $X$, where $T$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given $X$. We show that computing the optimal value $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R) = \sup_T \{ I(Y;T) : I(X;T) \le R \}$ of the information bottleneck problem, as well as its Lagrangian relaxation $L_β(P_{XY}) = \sup_T \big[I(Y;T) - βI(X;T)\big]$, is NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$, neither $\mathrm{IB}(P_{XY},R)$ nor $L_β(P_{XY})$ can be approximated in polynomial time within an additive error of order $|\mathcal{X}|^{-3/2}$.

title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
summary: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.

title: ExecWeave: Cross-Layer Execution Provenance for Observable Agentic Software
summary:
Agentic software invokes tools, launches processes, accesses files, and communicates with local or remote services. Application traces describe logical operations, whereas operating-system telemetry records machine activity without necessarily identifying the responsible agent action. Relating these evidence planes is a reconstruction problem: a plausible but unsupported association can assign an effect to the wrong principal.
  We present ExecWeave, a local-first system that materializes provider semantics and independently observed runtime events into a typed execution graph. The implementation retains separate source artifacts, distinguishes logical occurrences from repeated evidence, and records attribution, inference, and causal-status metadata. An optional command-to-process correlator emits a non-causal inferred bridge only when its bounded search yields one compatible observed process; uniqueness within this observed candidate set is not a guarantee of causal correctness. OS-observed file and network effects acquire a semantic tool or agent principal only through an observed process plus a justified command-to-process association; session-correlated file-system events do not by themselves provide that principal.
  Source code is available at https://github.com/Irish-kw/ExecWeave.

title: Seeing Through Sparse Signals: CS-Enhanced Sensing With QoS Guarantees for 6G ISAC
summary: In integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, communication and sensing share time-frequency resources, creating a fundamental trade-off between communication quality of service (QoS) and quality of sensing (QoSe). Reusing 5G new radio (NR) reference signals (RSs) enables standard-compliant sensing, but their inherent sparsity leads to undersampled channels and strong sidelobes that degrade weak-target detection. Compressed sensing (CS) can mitigate these effects, yet existing methods either overlook communication QoS constraints or rely on reconstruction algorithms that are step-size-sensitive or employ global thresholding, leading to weak-target masking in multi-target scenarios. The multi-target detection problem, therefore, requires a joint design of resource scheduling and CS-based reconstruction. In this work, we investigate the impact of two scheduling schemes, namely QoS-guaranteed scheduling and proportional-fairness (PF)-based scheduling, on the sensing-communication trade-off. To further enhance sensing performance, we employ a 2D max-median complex approximate message passing (2D-mmCAMP) algorithm that performs adaptive row- and column-wise thresholding to suppress sidelobes while preserving weak-target responses in multi-target scenarios. Simulations demonstrate an improvement of >= 16% in weak-target detection over baseline reconstruction algorithms while meeting downlink (DL) QoS constraints, validating the effectiveness of the proposed NR-compliant ISAC scheme.

title: When Fresh Information Is Not Enough: Age-of-Actuation-Optimal Scheduling for Energy-Harvesting Actuators
summary: We study transmission scheduling in an energy-harvesting actuation system where an actuation requires both a received update and available energy. While age of information (AoI) measures information freshness, age of actuation (AoA) measures the time elapsed since the latest completed actuation. The transmitter observes the receiver's AoA and battery state and decides whether to transmit a fresh update in each slot. We formulate average-AoA minimization as a Markov decision process and establish an AoA-threshold property for an optimal policy. We also derive the average AoA in closed form under the AoI-optimal policy, which is always-transmit.
